title: Using hollow wall anchors on plasterboard
subtitle: Choose the right fixing type for the load and wall construction, drill, insert, and set hollow-wall anchors for shelves, mirrors, and wall-mounted fittings
excerpt: How to fix to a hollow plasterboard wall using cavity anchors. Covers fixing types (toggle bolts, spring toggles, metal sleeve anchors, resin capsules), drilling to the right depth, and setting the anchor for the load.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). Black and Decker Complete Photo Guide to Home Improvement (referenced, not reproduced). UK fixing manufacturers' technical guidance (open access).

glossaryTerms.definition: A fixing designed to grip the back face of a hollow wall panel (plasterboard or similar) by expanding, toggling, or spreading behind the board. Includes spring toggle bolts, metal sleeve anchors (such as Grip-it or Fischer Duoblade), and nylon cavity plugs. Rated to a maximum load that must not be exceeded.

An electronic tool that detects the timber studs or metal channels behind plasterboard by sensing changes in density. Used to locate stud positions before drilling, so fixings can be made directly into timber where higher loads are needed.

content.text: A hollow plasterboard wall has no solid core to grip a conventional screw; the screw simply pulls through.

solve this by bearing against the back face of the board. The technique is: choose the anchor for the load, drill the correct hole, insert and set. The right anchor for a light mirror is different from the right anchor for a heavy shelf.
Locate studs and check the wall construction

or knock the wall and listen for the hollow sound between studs. For heavy loads (more than 10 kg per fixing), fix into a timber stud using a 3.5 or 4 mm wood screw. A screw into a stud is ten times stronger than a cavity anchor in the same board. Save cavity anchors for positions where there is no stud available.

Metal sleeve anchor (Fischer Duoblade or Grip-it type): the most reliable for medium loads (up to 25 kg per fixing). A metal collar unfolds behind the board as the screw is tightened. Requires a precise hole diameter (usually 10 or 13 mm). Self-drilling versions remove the drill step.

Nylon cavity plug (snap-toggle or spring wing): adequate for light loads (mirrors, small shelves, picture frames up to about 10 kg). Insert through a 10 mm hole; the wings open behind the board and grip as the screw is tightened.

Spring toggle (metal): the traditional heavy fixing. Insert collapsed through a hole; the spring wings open behind the board. If the screw is removed, the toggle drops into the cavity. Suitable for loads up to 50 kg in standard 12.5 mm plasterboard.

Drill the pilot hole at the correct diameter for the anchor (stated on the packet). Use a sharp masonry bit for plasterboard; drill slowly to avoid crumbling the face paper. Do not use hammer action on plasterboard; it shatters the core. Insert the anchor and set it according to the type: sleeve anchors tighten with a screwdriver; spring toggles require a slight rearward pull as the screw is tightened to clamp the wings against the back face. A correctly set anchor feels solid and does not rotate when tapped.

attrs.symptom: The anchor spins in the hole when the screw is tightened
attrs.cause: The hole is slightly oversized, or the anchor type does not suit the board thickness.
attrs.fix: Use a larger-diameter anchor, or switch to a metal sleeve type that grips by mechanical expansion rather than by friction.

attrs.symptom: The board cracks around the anchor after fitting a load
attrs.cause: The load exceeded the anchor's rated capacity, or multiple anchors were placed too close together.
attrs.fix: Fix into a timber stud instead, or spread the load across more anchors spaced at least 150 mm apart.
